disease.name: Arthritis
disease.icd_10_code: M00-M25 (varies by type: OA M15-M19; RA M05-M06; Gout M10; PsA M07)

overview.description: Arthritis is not a single disease but an umbrella term for more than 100 different conditions that cause pain, swelling, stiffness, and decreased range of motion in one or more joints. The two most common forms are Osteoarthritis (OA) — a degenerative 'wear and tear' disease caused by cartilage breakdown — and Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) — a chronic autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks the joint lining (synovium). Arthritis is the leading cause of disability in adults worldwide, significantly impacting daily activities, quality of life, and work productivity.
overview.affected_organ: Joints (synovium, cartilage, bone, tendons, ligaments); also systemic organs in inflammatory arthritis (heart, lungs, eyes, kidneys in RA)
overview.prevalence: Over 530 million people affected worldwide (WHO 2023); approximately 54 million adults in the USA (CDC); leading cause of disability globally.
overview.age_group: All age groups; OA predominantly affects adults over 50; RA most commonly onset 30-60 years; juvenile arthritis in children under 16.

types.name: Osteoarthritis (OA)
types.description: Most common form of arthritis (~80% of cases). Caused by progressive breakdown and eventual loss of articular cartilage in joints, resulting in bone-on-bone friction, osteophyte (bone spur) formation, joint space narrowing, and subchondral bone changes. Primarily a mechanical and metabolic disease, though inflammation is also present.
types.common_in: Adults over 50; women more than men after menopause; obese individuals; athletes with prior joint injuries

types.name: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
types.description: Chronic systemic autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks the synovial membrane lining the joints, causing persistent synovitis, pannus formation, progressive joint destruction, deformity, and disability. Characterized by symmetrical small joint involvement, morning stiffness lasting >1 hour, and elevated inflammatory markers. Can affect multiple organ systems beyond joints.
types.common_in: Women 3x more than men; age 30-60 (can occur at any age); strong genetic association (HLA-DR4, DR1)

types.name: Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA)
types.description: Inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis (chronic skin condition causing red, scaly patches). Affects approximately 30% of people with psoriasis. Can affect any joint; distinguished by dactylitis (sausage digit — swelling of entire finger or toe), nail pitting, and enthesitis (inflammation at tendon/ligament insertion points). Seronegative (RF negative).
most_affected_joints: Any joint — asymmetric pattern; DIP joints characteristically; sacroiliac joints; spine
types.common_in: Adults with psoriasis; age 30-55; equal male-female ratio

types.name: Gout
types.scientific_name: Gouty Arthritis / Monosodium Urate Crystal Arthropathy
types.description: Caused by deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joints and soft tissues due to hyperuricemia (elevated serum uric acid). Presents as sudden, excruciatingly painful, hot, swollen, red joints (flares) — classically the first metatarsophalangeal joint (big toe = podagra). Crystals form tophi (hard deposits) over time. Triggered by high-purine foods, alcohol, dehydration, medications, and medical illness.
most_affected_joints: First MTP joint (big toe — podagra, most classic)
types.common_in: Men >40 years (women after menopause); individuals with hyperuricemia; those on diuretics or low-dose aspirin

types.name: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA)
types.description: The most common chronic arthritis in children under 16 years. Umbrella term for several subtypes of chronic childhood arthritis persisting for more than 6 weeks with no identifiable cause. Can cause joint damage, growth abnormalities, uveitis (eye inflammation), and disability if not treated promptly.
types.common_in: Children under 16 years; girls more common for most subtypes

types.name: Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) / Axial Spondyloarthritis (axSpA)
types.description: Chronic inflammatory arthritis primarily affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints, causing progressive spinal fusion (ankylosis), back pain, and postural changes (stooped posture — question mark spine). Associated with HLA-B27 gene marker. Also causes uveitis (eye), cardiac, and pulmonary complications. Part of the spondyloarthropathy family.
types.common_in: Young men aged 15-35; HLA-B27 positive individuals; male-to-female ratio 3:1

types.name: Reactive Arthritis (Reiter's Syndrome)
types.description: Sterile joint inflammation triggered by a preceding infection (usually genitourinary — Chlamydia, or gastrointestinal — Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter). Classic triad: arthritis + urethritis/cervicitis + conjunctivitis ('can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree'). Seronegative; HLA-B27 positive in 60-80%.
types.common_in: Young adults aged 20-40; more common in men after genitourinary infection; both sexes after GI infection

types.name: Septic Arthritis (Infectious Arthritis)
types.description: Medical emergency. Bacterial infection of a joint causing rapid, destructive inflammation. Can destroy the joint within days if untreated. Most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA). Hematogenous spread most common. Requires urgent joint aspiration, culture, and IV antibiotics.
types.common_in: Elderly, immunocompromised, IV drug users, patients with prosthetic joints, patients with pre-existing joint disease (RA, OA)

types.name: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Arthritis (Lupus Arthritis)
types.description: Joint involvement occurs in >90% of lupus patients. Arthritis is typically non-erosive and symmetrical (unlike RA). Jaccoud's arthropathy refers to reducible deformities from ligamentous laxity in SLE. Lupus is a systemic autoimmune disease also affecting kidneys, skin, heart, brain, and blood.
types.common_in: Women of childbearing age (15-45 years); 9:1 female-to-male ratio; African American, Hispanic, and Asian women disproportionately affected

types.name: Pseudogout (CPPD Disease)
types.description: Crystal-induced arthritis caused by deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals in joint cartilage and synovial fluid. Clinically similar to gout but often involves knees, wrists, and ankles rather than the big toe. Rhombus-shaped crystals (positively birefringent) on microscopy — distinguishes from gout (needle-shaped, negatively birefringent).
types.common_in: Elderly adults over 60; associated with hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypomagnesemia

severity_levels.name: Mild Arthritis
severity_levels.description: Occasional joint pain and stiffness with minimal functional limitation
severity_levels.functional_impact: Can perform all daily activities independently; some discomfort with prolonged activity
severity_levels.structural_changes: OA: Early joint space narrowing (Grade I Kellgren-Lawrence); RA: No erosions on X-ray (ACR/EULAR remission possible with early treatment)
severity_levels.management: NSAIDs or paracetamol as needed; physical therapy; lifestyle modifications; topical treatments; patient education

severity_levels.name: Moderate Arthritis
severity_levels.description: Regular pain and stiffness limiting some activities; swelling may be present
severity_levels.functional_impact: Difficulty with stairs, prolonged walking, lifting, and fine hand tasks; affects work and social activities
severity_levels.structural_changes: OA: Moderate joint space narrowing, early osteophytes (Grade II-III K-L); RA: Early erosions on X-ray; DAS28 score >3.2
severity_levels.management: Oral NSAIDs; intra-articular corticosteroid injections; DMARDs for RA/PsA; combination therapy; occupational therapy

severity_levels.name: Severe Arthritis
severity_levels.description: Constant or near-constant pain; significant deformity or joint destruction; major functional limitation
severity_levels.functional_impact: Unable to perform basic daily tasks independently; difficulty with personal care, walking, and employment
severity_levels.structural_changes: OA: Severe joint space loss, large osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis (Grade III-IV K-L); RA: Multiple erosions, joint deformities (swan neck, boutonniere, ulnar deviation)
severity_levels.management: Combination DMARDs or biologic agents (RA/PsA); strong analgesics; joint replacement surgery (OA); multidisciplinary team care; assistive devices

severity_levels.name: End-Stage / Refractory Arthritis
severity_levels.description: Complete joint destruction, severe deformity, or refractory disease not responding to standard treatment
severity_levels.pain_scale: 9-10 / 10 VAS; constant pain significantly impacting quality of life
severity_levels.functional_impact: Dependent on others for daily care; severe disability; unable to work or maintain independence
severity_levels.structural_changes: OA: Bone-on-bone articulation, joint collapse, severe malalignment; RA: Mutilans deformity; ankylosis in AS
severity_levels.management: Total joint replacement (arthroplasty) — knee, hip, shoulder; arthrodesis (joint fusion) for small joints; biologic/targeted synthetic DMARDs for inflammatory; palliative pain management; comprehensive rehabilitation

genetic_factors: HLA-DR4 and HLA-DR1 gene variants — strongly associated with seropositive Rheumatoid Arthritis
HLA-B27 — associated with Ankylosing Spondylitis, Reactive Arthritis, and Psoriatic Arthritis (axial)
Family history of arthritis — first-degree relatives have 3-5x increased risk of RA
PTPN22, PADI4, STAT4, CTLA4 gene variants — implicated in autoimmune arthritis risk
COL2A1 (collagen type II) gene mutations — predispose to early-onset osteoarthritis
Family history of gout or hyperuricemia — SLC2A9, ABCG2 gene variants affecting uric acid transport
Genetic predisposition to cartilage degradation and impaired repair mechanisms (OA)
environmental_and_mechanical_triggers: Joint overuse and repetitive stress (occupational or sporting activities) — accelerates cartilage wear (OA)
Previous joint injury or trauma — intra-articular fractures, ligament tears, meniscal damage increase OA risk 3-5x
Obesity — increases mechanical load on weight-bearing joints; also promotes systemic inflammation worsening both OA and RA
Sedentary lifestyle — muscle weakness, reduced joint stability
Smoking — strongest environmental risk factor for RA; increases anti-CCP antibody production via PADI4 activation in lungs

Infections — trigger Reactive Arthritis (Chlamydia, Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter); postulated role in RA via molecular mimicry (Epstein-Barr virus, Porphyromonas gingivalis in periodontitis)
High dietary purine intake (red meat, organ meats, shellfish, beer) — elevates uric acid levels causing gout
Alcohol — increases uric acid production and reduces renal excretion (gout trigger)
Dehydration — reduces uric acid excretion, precipitating gout attacks
Occupational hazards: heavy lifting, kneeling, squatting (miners, farmers, construction workers) — OA risk
Hormonal changes — estrogen decline after menopause dramatically increases OA and RA risk
Periodontitis (gum disease) — associated with increased RA susceptibility via citrullination by P. gingivalis bacteria
other_causes: Autoimmune dysregulation — immune system attacks self-antigens in synovial joint (RA, PsA, AS, SLE arthritis)
Crystal deposition — monosodium urate (gout), calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout), basic calcium phosphate
Bacterial joint infection — Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus, Gram-negative organisms (septic arthritis)
Viral joint infection — Parvovirus B19, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, chikungunya, rubella, HIV
Metabolic disorders — hyperuricemia (gout), hemochromatosis (iron overload), hyperparathyroidism, Wilson's disease
Medications — diuretics (thiazide, loop) and low-dose aspirin increase urate levels (gout); some medications trigger drug-induced lupus arthritis
Blood disorders — hemophilia (hemarthrosis), sickle cell disease
Neurological conditions — Charcot joint (neuropathic arthropathy) from diabetic neuropathy, syphilis
Prosthetic joint failure or infection (periprosthetic joint infection)

primary_symptoms.name: Joint Pain (Arthralgia)
primary_symptoms.description: Pain in one or more joints — may be aching, sharp, burning, or throbbing. In OA, pain worsens with activity and improves with rest. In RA, pain is present at rest and worse in the morning. In gout, pain is sudden and excruciating. Pain can be constant or episodic (flares).
primary_symptoms.onset: Gradual (OA, RA) or sudden (gout, septic arthritis, reactive arthritis)

primary_symptoms.name: Joint Stiffness
primary_symptoms.description: Reduced ability to move a joint through its full range of motion. Morning stiffness lasting >1 hour is a hallmark of inflammatory arthritis (RA, PsA, AS). In OA, stiffness is typically brief (<30 minutes, 'gelling effect') after rest, improving with movement.
primary_symptoms.onset: Worst in the morning or after periods of inactivity

primary_symptoms.name: Joint Swelling and Effusion
primary_symptoms.description: Visible or palpable swelling of the joint due to synovial thickening (inflammatory arthritis), joint effusion (fluid accumulation), or both. In RA — boggy, soft, warm swelling (synovitis). In OA — bony, hard enlargement (osteophytes). In gout — extremely swollen, hot, red, tender joint.
primary_symptoms.onset: Episodic in gout (acute flares); persistent in RA; gradual in OA

primary_symptoms.name: Warmth and Redness (Erythema) over Joint
primary_symptoms.description: Increased skin temperature and redness over the affected joint indicating active inflammation. Most prominent in gout (bright red), septic arthritis, and acute inflammatory RA flares. Less common in OA.

primary_symptoms.name: Reduced Range of Motion
primary_symptoms.description: Decreased ability to move the joint through its normal arc of movement due to pain, swelling, mechanical damage, or contracture. Measurable with goniometer. A key determinant of disability.
primary_symptoms.onset: Progressive in OA; variable in RA; may be abrupt in septic arthritis

primary_symptoms.name: Fatigue and Malaise
primary_symptoms.description: Profound tiredness and general feeling of being unwell — especially prominent in systemic inflammatory arthritis (RA, SLE arthritis, PsA). Driven by chronic inflammation (cytokines — TNF-α, IL-6), anemia of chronic disease, pain-disrupted sleep, and depression. Can be as debilitating as joint pain.

primary_symptoms.name: Joint Deformity
primary_symptoms.description: Visible structural changes to joint shape from cartilage/bone loss or soft tissue damage. In OA: Heberden's nodes (DIP joints), Bouchard's nodes (PIP joints), valgus/varus knee deformity. In RA: ulnar deviation of fingers, swan-neck deformity, boutonniere deformity, Z-thumb, subluxation.
primary_symptoms.severity: Moderate to Severe (irreversible in advanced disease)
primary_symptoms.onset: Late manifestation; months to years of progressive disease

secondary_symptoms: Crepitus — grating, clicking, or crackling sound/sensation in the joint during movement (OA hallmark)
Muscle weakness and wasting around affected joints from disuse
Difficulty sleeping due to joint pain and stiffness (nocturnal pain — especially hip OA, RA)
Depression and anxiety — common in chronic pain conditions; affects 20-30% of arthritis patients
Loss of appetite and unintentional weight loss in systemic inflammatory arthritis (RA)
Fever — low-grade in RA flares; high fever in septic arthritis, systemic JIA, reactive arthritis
Nodules — rheumatoid nodules (firm subcutaneous lumps over pressure points — elbows, fingers; RA); tophi (gout)
Dry eyes and dry mouth (Sjögren's syndrome overlap with RA)
Skin rashes — butterfly facial rash (lupus arthritis); psoriatic plaques (PsA); keratoderma (reactive arthritis)
Nail changes — pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis (PsA)
Anaemia of chronic disease — fatigue, pallor, reduced exercise capacity (common in RA)
Carpal tunnel syndrome — entrapment of median nerve from wrist joint swelling (RA)
Tendon rupture — especially extensor tendons of fingers in advanced RA
warning_signs_of_attack: Sudden onset extremely severe joint pain — especially if new, single joint (rule out septic arthritis / gout)
Red, hot, swollen joint with fever — septic arthritis until proven otherwise (joint destruction within 24-48h)
Loss of ability to bear weight on leg or use affected limb
New joint swelling with skin warmth after a recent infection (throat, genitourinary, gastrointestinal)
Severe spine pain with neurological symptoms (numbness, weakness, bladder/bowel changes) — AS with cord compression
Sudden loss of range of motion in a previously functioning joint
symptoms_in_children: Persistent joint swelling for more than 6 weeks without clear injury (JIA hallmark)
Joint stiffness and limping in the morning; improving throughout the day with activity
Reluctance to walk, use affected limb, or engage in physical activities
Unexplained fevers — especially spiking fever with salmon-colored rash (systemic JIA/Still's disease)
Eye redness, pain, or vision changes — anterior uveitis (30% of oligoarticular JIA); may be asymptomatic
Unequal limb lengths or joint enlargement due to altered growth patterns near inflamed growth plates
Fatigue, irritability, and poor school performance from chronic pain and disrupted sleep

osteoarthritis: Pain worse with weight-bearing activity, climbing stairs, and prolonged standing; relieved by rest
Heberden's nodes (bony swelling at DIP joints) and Bouchard's nodes (PIP joints) in hand OA
Crepitus on knee examination — palpable grinding during flexion-extension
No or minimal systemic symptoms (no significant fever, no elevated inflammatory markers usually)
Bilateral knee pain with varus (bow-legged) deformity in medial compartment knee OA
rheumatoid_arthritis: Symmetrical joint involvement — both wrists, both MCP joints, both knees
Morning stiffness lasting >1 hour — characteristic and essential diagnostic feature
Extra-articular features: rheumatoid nodules, Sjögren's overlap, interstitial lung disease, pericarditis, vasculitis, episcleritis
Elevated CRP, ESR, positive RF (rheumatoid factor), and anti-CCP antibodies
Anemia of chronic disease; thrombocytosis during active disease
Atlanto-axial subluxation (C1-C2 instability) — rare but dangerous RA complication
gout_specific: Classic podagra — sudden, exquisite pain in first metatarsophalangeal joint (big toe) at night
Tophi — hard chalky deposits under skin at ear helix, olecranon bursa, Achilles tendon, finger joints
Hyperuricemia (serum uric acid >6.8 mg/dL) — prerequisite for urate crystal formation
Attacks often triggered by specific events: alcohol binge, high-purine meal, dehydration, acute illness, diuretic use
ankylosing_spondylitis_specific: Inflammatory back pain — insidious onset in young adults, improves with exercise (unlike mechanical back pain which worsens)
Bilateral sacroiliac joint tenderness on examination
Chest wall pain and restricted chest expansion (costovertebral joint involvement)
Iritis/uveitis — sudden painful red eye; occurs in 25-40% of AS patients
Progressive spinal fusion causing reduced spinal mobility and 'question mark' posture in late disease

medical_history: Detailed joint symptom history — onset, duration, pattern (symmetrical/asymmetrical, migratory/additive), morning stiffness duration
Family history of arthritis, autoimmune diseases, psoriasis, or gout
Prior joint injuries, surgeries, or infections
Occupation and physical activity history (joint overuse, repetitive strain)
Current medications — especially diuretics, low-dose aspirin, ciclosporin, ethambutol (uric acid raising)
Dietary history — purine-rich food and alcohol intake (gout assessment)
Sexual and gastrointestinal infection history (reactive arthritis)
Skin disease (psoriasis), eye disease (uveitis), gut disease (IBD) — spondyloarthropathy screen
Comorbidities: cardiovascular disease, diabetes, hypertension, renal disease
physical_examination: Joint inspection — swelling, deformity, skin changes, muscle wasting, nodules, tophi, rashes
Joint palpation — warmth, tenderness, synovial thickening (boggy vs bony), effusion detection
Range of motion assessment — active and passive, with goniometer measurement
Special joint tests: McMurray's test (knee meniscus), Lachman's test (ACL), Finkelstein's test (De Quervain's), FABER test (hip/SI joint), Schober's test (lumbar spine mobility — AS screening)
Gait assessment — antalgic gait (pain avoidance), Trendelenburg gait (hip abductor weakness)
Grip strength assessment — dynamometer or functional test (jar opening, handshake)
Neurological examination — for neuropathic pain, carpal tunnel signs (Tinel's, Phalen's), radiculopathy
Skin examination — psoriatic plaques, rheumatoid nodules, rashes, tophi
Eye examination — conjunctivitis (reactive arthritis), uveitis (AS, JIA), episcleritis (RA)
Chest examination — reduced chest expansion (AS); pleural effusion, pericardial rub (RA)
Cardiovascular assessment — aortic regurgitation murmur (AS); pericarditis (RA, SLE)
Functional assessment — HAQ (Health Assessment Questionnaire) for daily living activities

diagnostic_tests.description: Autoantibody (usually IgM) directed against the Fc portion of IgG. Positive in 70-80% of RA patients (seropositive RA). Also positive in other autoimmune conditions, infections, and 5% of healthy population.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Supports diagnosis of Rheumatoid Arthritis; prognostic marker (high titer RF — worse prognosis)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive: >14 IU/mL (lab-dependent); high titer >100 IU/mL associated with aggressive erosive disease

diagnostic_tests.description: Highly specific autoantibody for Rheumatoid Arthritis. More specific than RF (~95% specificity). Can be positive years before clinical RA onset. Predicts severe erosive disease and poor prognosis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Most specific serological marker for RA; confirms RA diagnosis; predicts erosive disease
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive: >17 U/mL (varies by lab); sensitivity 67-70%, specificity ~95% for RA

diagnostic_tests.description: Non-specific marker of systemic inflammation. Elevated in inflammatory arthritis (RA, PsA, AS), infection, and malignancy. Normal in OA (distinguishes inflammatory from non-inflammatory arthritis).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess inflammatory activity; monitor treatment response; distinguish inflammatory from non-inflammatory arthritis
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal: <15 mm/hr (men), <20 mm/hr (women); elevated in inflammatory arthritis (often >40-100 mm/hr in active RA)

diagnostic_tests.description: Acute phase protein produced by liver in response to inflammation. More sensitive and faster-responding than ESR. Rises within hours of inflammation onset. Used in DAS28 disease activity score calculation for RA.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess disease activity; monitor treatment response; detect flares and infections
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal: <5 mg/L (high-sensitivity CRP <1 mg/L); active RA: typically >10-50 mg/L

diagnostic_tests.description: Measures blood uric acid concentration. Hyperuricemia (elevated uric acid) is a prerequisite for gout, but not all hyperuricemic patients develop gout. May be normal during acute gout attack (urate shifts into crystals).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screens for and monitors hyperuricemia in gout; guides urate-lowering therapy
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal: <6.8 mg/dL in women, <7.0 mg/dL in men; hyperuricemia: >6.8 mg/dL; treatment target: <5-6 mg/dL

diagnostic_tests.description: Detects presence of HLA-B27 histocompatibility antigen. Present in 90-95% of Ankylosing Spondylitis patients, 60-80% of Reactive Arthritis, and some PsA with axial involvement. Present in 8% of general population.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Supports diagnosis of spondyloarthropathies (AS, ReA); not diagnostic alone
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive or Negative. Positive strongly supports AS diagnosis in context of clinical features and MRI changes

diagnostic_tests.description: Screens for autoimmune conditions, especially systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Positive in SLE, RA, Sjögren's, scleroderma, and other connective tissue diseases. Also positive in ~10% healthy population.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for systemic autoimmune disease; positive ANA triggers further specific antibody testing
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Titer ≥1:80 considered positive; high titer (1:320 or greater) more clinically significant

diagnostic_tests.description: Provides comprehensive blood cell analysis. In inflammatory arthritis: normocytic normochromic anemia (anemia of chronic disease); thrombocytosis during active inflammation; leukopenia in SLE (Felty's syndrome in RA).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess for anemia, infection, baseline before DMARD therapy; monitor side effects of DMARDs
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Anemia (Hb <12 g/dL women, <13 g/dL men); thrombocytosis (platelets >400×10⁹/L in active RA)

diagnostic_tests.description: Standard first-line imaging for arthritis. Shows joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and cysts (OA). Shows periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions in RA. Calcification in CPPD. Radiographic changes lag behind clinical disease by months-years.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm diagnosis, assess disease severity and progression, plan surgical intervention
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Kellgren-Lawrence Grading (OA, 0-4): Grade 0 (normal) to Grade 4 (severe — bone-on-bone, large osteophytes); Larsen Score (RA erosions)

diagnostic_tests.description: Gold standard for early detection of inflammatory arthritis and sacroiliitis. Detects synovitis, bone marrow edema (earliest sign of sacroiliitis in AS), cartilage damage, tendon pathology, and erosions before X-ray changes appear. Essential for early RA and AS diagnosis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect early disease (before X-ray changes); assess soft tissue structures; guide treatment decisions
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Bone marrow edema on STIR sequences: early sacroiliitis sign in AS; gadolinium-enhanced: active synovitis in RA

diagnostic_tests.description: Real-time imaging of joint synovitis, effusions, tendons, bursae, and entheses. Power Doppler detects active synovial vascularity (active inflammation). Guides joint aspiration and injection procedures.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect synovitis, effusions, and enthesitis; assess disease activity; guide injections
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Synovial thickness >2mm with power Doppler signal = active synovitis; useful for monitoring treatment response

diagnostic_tests.description: Aspiration of synovial fluid from the joint for cell count, differential, culture, and crystal analysis. Essential for excluding septic arthritis (emergency) and confirming crystal arthritis (gout, CPPD).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: ESSENTIAL for excluding septic arthritis; confirms crystal arthritis; differentiates inflammatory from non-inflammatory
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal: WBC <200/µL; Non-inflammatory (OA): 200-2000/µL; Inflammatory (RA): 2000-50,000/µL; Septic: >50,000/µL with predominantly neutrophils; Gout: needle-shaped negatively birefringent MSU crystals; CPPD: rhomboid positively birefringent CPP crystals

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Liver Function Tests (LFTs) and Renal Function
diagnostic_tests.description: Baseline and monitoring tests required before and during DMARD therapy. Methotrexate can cause hepatotoxicity; NSAIDs cause renal impairment and GI toxicity; leflunomide can cause liver damage.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Baseline assessment; monitor for DMARD hepatotoxicity and renal toxicity; eGFR for dose adjustment
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: ALT/AST >3x upper limit normal: halt methotrexate; eGFR <30 mL/min: avoid NSAIDs, adjust DMARD dosing

diagnostic_tests.description: Measures bone mineral density at lumbar spine and hip. Patients with inflammatory arthritis on corticosteroids have significantly increased osteoporosis risk.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect and monitor corticosteroid-induced osteoporosis; fracture risk assessment

diagnostic_tests.test_name: TB Screening (Mantoux / IGRA) and Hepatitis B/C Serology
diagnostic_tests.description: Mandatory screening before starting biologic DMARD therapy (TNF inhibitors). TNF blockers reactivate latent TB. Hepatitis B reactivation is a serious risk with rituximab and other biologics.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Mandatory pre-biologic screening; prevents life-threatening TB reactivation
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold) or Mantoux >5mm: latent TB prophylaxis required before biologics

medicines.note: All medications must be prescribed and supervised by a licensed rheumatologist or physician. Arthritis medications carry significant risks and require regular monitoring. Self-medication is dangerous. Treatment must be individualized based on arthritis type, severity, comorbidities, and patient preference.

categories.purpose: Relieve joint pain and reduce fever. First-line for mild to moderate osteoarthritis.

medicines.name: Paracetamol / Acetaminophen
medicines.dosage: 500-1000 mg every 4-6 hours; maximum 4000 mg/day (3000 mg/day in liver disease or elderly)
medicines.use_case: First-line pain relief for mild OA; preferred in elderly and patients with cardiovascular disease or peptic ulcers who cannot tolerate NSAIDs
side_effects: Minimal side effects at recommended doses
medicines.note: Less effective for inflammatory arthritis than NSAIDs; does not reduce joint swelling or stiffness

medicines.name: Tramadol
medicines.dosage: 50-100 mg every 4-6 hours (IR); 100-200 mg twice daily (SR); max 400 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Moderate to severe OA pain when NSAIDs contraindicated; short-term use; adjunct therapy
medicines.note: Opioid analgesic — use with caution; avoid in elderly (fall risk); not for long-term first-line use

categories.purpose: Reduce joint pain, swelling, and stiffness by inhibiting COX-1 and/or COX-2 enzymes, blocking prostaglandin synthesis. First-line for inflammatory arthritis symptom control.

medicines.name: Ibuprofen
medicines.dosage: 400-800 mg three times daily with food; max 2400-3200 mg/day; topical: apply 3-4x daily
medicines.use_case: Mild to moderate arthritis pain and inflammation; widely used first-line NSAID
side_effects: GI upset, ulcers, and bleeding (most common)
medicines.monitoring: Renal function, blood pressure; use lowest effective dose for shortest duration

medicines.name: Naproxen
medicines.dosage: 250-500 mg twice daily with food; max 1000 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Arthritis pain and inflammation; relatively lower cardiovascular risk compared to other NSAIDs

medicines.name: Diclofenac
medicines.form: Tablet, SR Tablet, Injection, Topical gel/patch
medicines.dosage: 50 mg three times daily or 75 mg SR twice daily; topical gel: apply 2-4x daily to affected joint
medicines.use_case: OA (especially topical for knee and hand OA), RA, gout acute flares
side_effects: Hepatotoxicity (relatively higher than other NSAIDs — monitor LFTs)
medicines.note: Topical diclofenac gel preferred for knee/hand OA — reduced systemic side effects while maintaining local efficacy

medicines.name: Celecoxib
medicines.dosage: 100-200 mg once or twice daily
medicines.use_case: OA and RA; preferred in patients at high GI risk (ulcer history); COX-2 selective — reduced GI ulceration risk
side_effects: Reduced GI ulceration vs non-selective NSAIDs

medicines.name: Etoricoxib
medicines.dosage: 30-60 mg once daily (OA); 90 mg once daily (RA, acute gout flare)
medicines.use_case: OA, RA, acute gout attacks; COX-2 selective — lower GI risk

medicines.name: Indomethacin
medicines.dosage: 25-50 mg three times daily; max 200 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Particularly effective for acute gout attacks and AS (spondyloarthropathy); one of the most potent NSAIDs
medicines.note: Avoid in elderly; use short-term for gout flares

categories.purpose: Potent anti-inflammatory agents used to rapidly suppress inflammation in acute flares, bridge therapy until DMARDs take effect, and intra-articular local treatment.
categories.note: Long-term systemic corticosteroids should be avoided or minimized due to serious side effects.

medicines.name: Prednisolone
medicines.dosage: Low dose: 5-10 mg/day (RA bridge therapy); Moderate: 20-40 mg/day (acute flare); High: 0.5-1 mg/kg/day (severe vasculitis); taper gradually
medicines.use_case: RA — bridge therapy until DMARDs take effect; acute inflammatory flares; PsA; vasculitis; JIA
medicines.monitoring: Blood glucose, blood pressure, weight, bone density (DEXA), eye pressure with prolonged use

medicines.name: Methylprednisolone (IV Pulse)
medicines.form: IV Injection, IM Injection (Depo-Medrol for intra-articular)
medicines.dosage: IV pulse: 500-1000 mg IV over 30 minutes for 3 days (severe RA flare, vasculitis); IM: 80-120 mg (depot injection for acute flare); intra-articular: 10-40 mg per joint
medicines.use_case: Severe acute RA flare; intra-articular injection for single inflamed joint; before DMARD treatment takes effect
side_effects: All systemic steroid effects with long-term use

medicines.name: Triamcinolone Acetonide
medicines.dosage: Large joint (knee, hip, shoulder): 20-40 mg per injection; Small joint (wrist, finger): 10 mg
medicines.use_case: Intra-articular injection for single or oligoarticular OA flares, RA, gout — powerful local anti-inflammatory effect
side_effects: Skin depigmentation and fat atrophy at injection site
Cartilage damage with repeated frequent injections (limit to 3-4 per joint per year)
medicines.note: Joint aspiration followed by injection provides immediate relief and diagnostic information

medicines.name: Betamethasone
medicines.dosage: 3-12 mg per joint depending on size
medicines.use_case: Alternative intra-articular steroid; long-acting; effective for OA and inflammatory arthritis joints

categories.category_name: Conventional Synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs) — Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs
categories.purpose: Modify the underlying disease process, reduce inflammation, prevent joint damage, and achieve sustained remission in inflammatory arthritis (RA, PsA, JIA). Slow-acting — weeks to months for full effect.
categories.note: First-line disease-modifying therapy for RA and PsA. Early initiation (treat-to-target) within 3 months of diagnosis significantly improves long-term outcomes.

medicines.name: Methotrexate (MTX)
medicines.dosage: Start: 7.5-10 mg once weekly; increase by 2.5-5 mg every 4-8 weeks; usual maintenance: 15-25 mg once weekly; always with folic acid 5 mg once weekly (not on MTX day)
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE csDMARD for RA, PsA, JIA; anchor drug for combination csDMARD therapy; also used in AS as adjunct
medicines.mechanism: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) and thymidylate synthase; blocks folate-dependent cellular proliferation and purine synthesis; anti-inflammatory via adenosine pathway
side_effects: Nausea and GI upset (most common; folic acid reduces this)
Liver fibrosis and cirrhosis (monitor with LFTs; rare with low-dose weekly regimen)
Teratogenicity — CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy; must stop 3-6 months before conception
medicines.monitoring: LFTs and CBC every 4-8 weeks initially; every 3 months when stable; chest X-ray baseline; renal function

medicines.name: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ)
medicines.dosage: 200-400 mg daily (≤5 mg/kg/day — weight-based dosing to reduce retinal toxicity risk)
medicines.use_case: Mild RA (often combined with MTX and sulfasalazine in triple therapy); SLE arthritis; reduces cardiovascular risk in RA; anti-malarial with anti-inflammatory properties
medicines.mechanism: Inhibits toll-like receptor signaling; reduces antigen presentation; alkalinizes lysosomes; inhibits cytokine production
side_effects: Retinal toxicity (maculopathy — rare but irreversible; annual eye examination after 5 years)
Cardiac conduction abnormalities (rare; baseline ECG in patients with cardiac disease)
medicines.monitoring: Annual ophthalmology review (fundus, visual fields, OCT) from year 5 onwards

medicines.name: Sulfasalazine (SSZ)
medicines.dosage: Start 500 mg daily; increase by 500 mg/week to maintenance 1000-1500 mg twice daily (2-3 g/day total)
medicines.use_case: RA (combined with MTX and HCQ as triple therapy); PsA peripheral joint disease; early RA as monotherapy; AS peripheral arthritis
medicines.mechanism: Cleaved in colon to sulfapyridine and 5-aminosalicylic acid; reduces inflammatory mediators
side_effects: GI intolerance (nausea, abdominal pain) — enteric coating reduces this
Orange discoloration of urine and tears (harmless)
medicines.monitoring: CBC and LFTs every 4 weeks for first 3 months; then every 3 months

medicines.name: Leflunomide
medicines.dosage: Loading dose: 100 mg/day for 3 days (optional); maintenance: 10-20 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: RA and PsA; alternative to MTX when MTX is contraindicated or not tolerated; can be combined with MTX for inadequate responders
medicines.mechanism: Prodrug; active metabolite (teriflunomide) inhibits pyrimidine synthesis, blocking T-lymphocyte proliferation
side_effects: Teratogenic — long half-life; washout procedure required before conception
medicines.monitoring: LFTs, CBC, blood pressure every 4-8 weeks initially; drug washout with cholestyramine if switching

categories.purpose: Precisely targeted monoclonal antibodies or fusion proteins that block specific cytokines or immune pathways driving joint inflammation and destruction. Used for moderate-severe RA, PsA, AS not responding to csDMARDs.
categories.note: Require mandatory pre-treatment screening (TB, hepatitis B, hepatitis C). Increase risk of serious infections. Annual flu vaccine and pneumococcal vaccine required. Avoid live vaccines.

medicines.name: Adalimumab
medicines.dosage: 40 mg every 2 weeks (RA, PsA, AS); 80 mg loading then 40 mg every 2 weeks
medicines.use_case: RA, PsA, AS, JIA — most widely used anti-TNF biologic; effective for all phenotypes of spondyloarthropathy
medicines.mechanism: Anti-TNF-α monoclonal antibody; binds and neutralizes soluble and membrane-bound TNF-alpha
side_effects: Increased infection risk (TB reactivation, bacterial, fungal)
medicines.monitoring: TB and hepatitis screening before starting; CBC, LFTs every 3-6 months; no live vaccines during treatment
contraindications: Active tuberculosis or untreated latent TB

medicines.name: Etanercept
medicines.dosage: 50 mg once weekly or 25 mg twice weekly (RA, PsA, AS)
medicines.use_case: RA, PsA, AS, JIA (age ≥2 years); fusion protein — different mechanism from monoclonal antibodies
medicines.mechanism: TNF receptor fusion protein (TNFR2-Fc); decoys TNF molecules preventing receptor binding
medicines.note: Lower hepatitis B reactivation risk than other TNF inhibitors

medicines.name: Infliximab
medicines.dosage: 3-5 mg/kg IV at weeks 0, 2, 6 then every 8 weeks (RA — usually combined with MTX; AS; PsA)
medicines.use_case: RA, AS, PsA — IV administration suitable for patients unable to self-inject; used with MTX in RA to prevent immunogenicity
medicines.mechanism: Chimeric anti-TNF-α monoclonal antibody (75% human, 25% murine)
medicines.monitoring: Pre-infusion vital signs; TB and hepatitis screening pre-treatment

medicines.name: Tocilizumab
medicines.dosage: IV: 4-8 mg/kg every 4 weeks; SC: 162 mg every 1-2 weeks
medicines.use_case: Moderate-severe RA — effective as monotherapy (anti-IL-6 mechanism is highly effective without MTX); systemic JIA; GCA (giant cell arteritis)
medicines.mechanism: Anti-IL-6 receptor (anti-IL-6R) monoclonal antibody; blocks IL-6 signaling — key pro-inflammatory cytokine in RA
side_effects: Masks fever (reduces CRP — careful in infection monitoring)
medicines.monitoring: CBC, LFTs, lipids, CRP every 4-8 weeks initially

medicines.name: Abatacept
medicines.dosage: IV: weight-based (~10 mg/kg) monthly; SC: 125 mg weekly
medicines.use_case: Moderate-severe RA not responding to or intolerant of TNF inhibitors; PsA; JIA
medicines.mechanism: T-cell costimulation inhibitor; CTLA4-Ig fusion protein blocks CD80/CD86 — CD28 interaction on T cells, preventing T-cell activation
medicines.note: Particularly suitable for anti-CCP positive RA and patients with prior serious infections or recurrent infections on TNF inhibitors

medicines.name: Rituximab
medicines.dosage: 1000 mg IV on day 1 and day 15 (one course); repeat every 6-12 months as needed
medicines.use_case: Moderate-severe RA after failure of one or more TNF inhibitors; RA with lymphoma; RA with prior severe infection limiting TNF use
medicines.mechanism: Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody; depletes CD20+ B-lymphocytes, reducing autoantibody (RF, anti-CCP) production and B-cell mediated inflammation
side_effects: Infusion reactions (give IV methylprednisolone and antihistamine premedication)
Infection risk — hepatitis B reactivation (screen essential)
medicines.monitoring: Hepatitis B serology MANDATORY before starting; immunoglobulin levels with repeated courses; no live vaccines

medicines.name: Secukinumab
medicines.dosage: 150-300 mg SC at weeks 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (loading), then every 4 weeks (maintenance)
medicines.use_case: Ankylosing Spondylitis and PsA — highly effective; also RA; anti-IL-17A mechanism
medicines.mechanism: Anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody; blocks IL-17A, a key cytokine in spondyloarthropathies
side_effects: Inflammatory bowel disease worsening (avoid in IBD-associated PsA/AS)
medicines.note: Do not use in patients with active Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis

medicines.name: Ixekizumab
medicines.dosage: 160 mg SC loading, then 80 mg every 4 weeks (PsA, AS)
medicines.use_case: PsA and AS; particularly effective for skin and joint disease in PsA
medicines.mechanism: Anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody (same class as secukinumab; different binding epitope)

medicines.name: Guselkumab
medicines.dosage: 100 mg SC at weeks 0 and 4, then every 8 weeks
medicines.use_case: PsA — joint and skin manifestations; anti-IL-23 mechanism provides durable response
medicines.mechanism: Anti-IL-23 (p19 subunit) monoclonal antibody; blocks IL-23 signaling, key driver of Th17 pathway in PsA

categories.purpose: Orally administered small molecule drugs that inhibit Janus kinase (JAK) enzymes inside cells, blocking multiple cytokine signaling pathways simultaneously. Rapid onset of action (1-2 weeks). Alternative to biologics.
categories.note: FDA/EMA have issued warnings about cardiovascular risk, malignancy risk, thromboembolism, and opportunistic infections with JAK inhibitors. Careful patient selection required.

medicines.name: Tofacitinib
medicines.dosage: 5 mg twice daily (IR) or 11 mg once daily (XR) for RA and PsA
medicines.use_case: Moderate-severe RA after inadequate response to MTX; PsA; UC (different indication/dose)
medicines.mechanism: JAK1/JAK3 inhibitor; blocks signaling of IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21 — reduces T-cell and B-cell activation
side_effects: Serious infections (TB, herpes zoster — varicella zoster reactivation)
Cardiovascular events (increased MI risk vs TNF inhibitors in high-risk patients — ORAL Surveillance study)
Malignancy (higher lymphoma and lung cancer risk)
medicines.monitoring: Pre-treatment TB, hepatitis B/C screening; CBC, LFTs, lipids at baseline and regularly; avoid in patients with active infection, malignancy, cardiovascular risk
medicines.black_box_warning: FDA black box warning: serious infections, malignancy, thrombosis, cardiovascular events, mortality

medicines.name: Baricitinib
medicines.dosage: 2 mg or 4 mg once daily (RA); 2 mg for moderate RA; 4 mg for severe active RA
medicines.use_case: Moderate-severe RA after inadequate response to MTX; can be used as monotherapy or with MTX
medicines.mechanism: JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor; blocks IL-6, IL-12, IL-23, type I IFN signaling
medicines.monitoring: Same as tofacitinib; renal dose adjustment required (eGFR <60)

medicines.name: Upadacitinib
medicines.dosage: 15 mg once daily (RA, PsA, AS); 30 mg once daily for severe active RA or AS/PsA unresponsive to TNF inhibitors
medicines.use_case: RA, PsA, AS — highly selective JAK1 inhibitor; also approved for Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis
medicines.mechanism: Selective JAK1 inhibitor; blocks signaling of IL-6, IL-17, IFN-γ — strong anti-inflammatory effect
side_effects: Herpes zoster (shingles) reactivation (higher rate than other JAK inhibitors)
medicines.monitoring: Pre-treatment TB screening; CBC, LFTs, lipids; varicella zoster vaccination before starting (live vaccine — must be administered before biologic/JAK inhibitor)

categories.purpose: Lower serum uric acid levels to below the saturation threshold, preventing urate crystal formation and depositing. Essential for chronic gout management and tophus reduction.
categories.note: Start ULT 2-4 weeks AFTER acute gout attack resolves. Cover initiation with prophylactic colchicine or NSAID for 3-6 months to prevent initiation flares.

medicines.name: Allopurinol
medicines.dosage: Start: 100 mg daily; increase by 100 mg every 2-4 weeks to achieve target uric acid <6 mg/dL; usual maintenance: 300-600 mg/day (max 900 mg/day in renal impairment — dose per eGFR)
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE urate-lowering therapy for gout; recurrent gout attacks (≥2/year); tophi; uric acid kidney stones; gout with renal impairment
medicines.mechanism: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor; blocks conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid
side_effects: Skin rash (2-3%; rarely severe — Stevens-Johnson Syndrome/DRESS)
Bone marrow suppression (rare — especially with azathioprine co-prescription)
medicines.monitoring: Uric acid level every 4-6 weeks until target; renal function; HLA-B*58:01 genetic testing recommended in Asian patients (Han Chinese, Korean, Thai) before starting — high risk of severe cutaneous reactions (SJS/DRESS)
medicines.important: Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS): rare but potentially fatal — stop immediately if severe skin reaction develops; HLA-B*58:01 screening reduces this risk in high-risk populations

medicines.name: Febuxostat
medicines.dosage: 40-80 mg once daily (start 40 mg; increase to 80 mg if target uric acid not achieved after 4 weeks)
medicines.use_case: Alternative to allopurinol; preferred when allopurinol not tolerated or contraindicated; can be used in mild-moderate renal impairment without dose adjustment
medicines.mechanism: Non-purine selective xanthine oxidase inhibitor
side_effects: Arthralgia and gout flares during initiation

Cardiovascular events — FDA warning: higher rate of cardiovascular death vs allopurinol in high-risk cardiac patients (CARES trial); avoid in established cardiovascular disease when alternative available
medicines.monitoring: Uric acid, LFTs, cardiovascular risk assessment

medicines.name: Colchicine
medicines.dosage: Acute gout: 1 mg immediately, then 0.5 mg 1 hour later (low-dose regimen — as effective as high-dose, fewer GI side effects); Prophylaxis: 0.5-1 mg daily for 3-6 months after initiating ULT
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE for acute gout attacks; prophylaxis during ULT initiation to prevent mobilization flares; Familial Mediterranean Fever; pericarditis
medicines.mechanism: Inhibits microtubule polymerization; blocks neutrophil migration into joints; prevents NLRP3 inflammasome activation — blocks MSU crystal-induced inflammation
side_effects: Diarrhea and GI upset (most common, especially at higher doses)
Muscle toxicity (myopathy) — especially with statin or ciclosporin co-prescription; use low dose
medicines.monitoring: Renal and hepatic function (dose reduction in renal impairment); avoid with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, etc.)

medicines.name: Pegloticase
medicines.dosage: 8 mg IV every 2 weeks (given in healthcare facility with monitoring)
medicines.use_case: Severe refractory gout with tophi not responding to allopurinol or febuxostat; rapidly dissolves large tophi
medicines.mechanism: Pegylated recombinant uricase enzyme that converts uric acid to allantoin (more soluble, easily excreted)
side_effects: Infusion reactions (anaphylaxis in 6%; pre-treat with antihistamine and steroid)
Immunogenicity (anti-drug antibodies reduce efficacy over time)
medicines.monitoring: Uric acid before each infusion (stop if rises >6 mg/dL — antibody formation); infusion reaction monitoring

categories.purpose: Restore joint lubrication in osteoarthritis by injecting hyaluronic acid (hyaluronan) into the knee joint to supplement depleted synovial fluid.

medicines.name: Hyaluronic Acid (Sodium Hyaluronate)
medicines.dosage: Single large-molecule injection (Durolane) OR 3-5 weekly injections (Synvisc, Hyalgan) into knee joint; repeat every 6 months to 1 year
medicines.use_case: Mild to moderate knee OA when NSAIDs are contraindicated or inadequate; bridges to joint replacement surgery
medicines.mechanism: Supplements depleted hyaluronic acid in synovial fluid; improves lubrication and shock absorption; may have mild anti-inflammatory effect
side_effects: Post-injection pain and swelling (pseudo-septic reaction — rare)
medicines.note: Evidence for efficacy is moderate and inconsistent; NICE (UK) does not routinely recommend; still widely used in clinical practice

categories.purpose: Localized pain relief applied directly to the skin over affected joint — reduced systemic side effects compared to oral medications.

medicines.name: Topical Diclofenac Gel / Solution
medicines.dosage: Apply 2-4 grams (2-4 cm strip) to affected joint 3-4 times daily
medicines.use_case: First-line for knee and hand OA in elderly and those with GI or cardiovascular risk

medicines.name: Topical Capsaicin
medicines.dosage: Apply thin layer to affected joint 3-4 times daily; initial burning sensation reduces with continued use (depletion of substance P)
medicines.use_case: OA of knee and hand; particularly useful for patients who cannot take oral medications; neuropathic pain component
side_effects: Initial burning and stinging (decreases with regular use)
Avoid contact with eyes and mucous membranes

medicines.name: Topical NSAIDs (Ketoprofen, Piroxicam, Indomethacin gels)
medicines.dosage: Apply to affected joint 2-3 times daily
medicines.use_case: OA pain; adjunct to oral treatment; reduces need for systemic NSAIDs
side_effects: Photosensitivity (ketoprofen — avoid sun exposure to application site)

categories.purpose: When conservative and medical management fails, surgical options restore function, relieve pain, and improve quality of life.
categories.note: Surgical referral should be made when conservative treatment has failed for 3-6 months, when pain is severe and constant, and when quality of life is significantly impaired.

medicines.name: Total Knee Arthroplasty (TKA — Knee Replacement)
medicines.use_case: End-stage knee OA (Kellgren-Lawrence Grade IV); severe pain, failed conservative therapy, significant functional limitation
medicines.outcome: 90%+ significant pain relief and function improvement; implant survival 15-20+ years
medicines.post_op: Physical therapy essential; deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis (LMWH); early mobilization; return to daily activities at 4-6 weeks

medicines.name: Total Hip Arthroplasty (THA — Hip Replacement)
medicines.use_case: End-stage hip OA or RA; avascular necrosis; severe pain unresponsive to medical management
medicines.outcome: Highly effective — pain relief >95%; improved walking, ADLs; implant survival 15-25+ years

medicines.name: Arthroscopy
medicines.use_case: Knee meniscal tears, loose bodies, synovial biopsy; limited role in pure OA (no longer routinely recommended for OA alone per NICE guidelines)
medicines.note: Diagnostic arthroscopy for synovial biopsy in inflammatory arthritis; therapeutic for mechanical problems

medicines.name: Arthrodesis (Joint Fusion)
medicines.use_case: End-stage small joint arthritis (wrist, ankle, subtalar) where arthroplasty not feasible; severe finger/wrist RA deformity; relieves pain by eliminating joint movement
medicines.note: Eliminates movement at fused joint but relieves pain permanently

medicines.name: Synovectomy
medicines.use_case: Persistent inflammatory synovitis in RA or PsA not responding to DMARDs in a single joint; particularly knee and wrist; delays joint destruction
medicines.note: Increasingly replaced by intra-articular biologics and improved DMARD therapies

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet plays a significant role in managing arthritis by reducing systemic inflammation (key in RA, PsA, AS, gout), supporting joint health (OA), controlling weight (reduces mechanical joint load), and minimizing medication side effects. The Mediterranean diet is the most evidence-based dietary pattern for arthritis management. For gout, strict dietary purine control is essential.

items.food: Fatty fish: Salmon, Mackerel, Sardines, Herring, Trout
items.benefit: Richest source of EPA and DHA omega-3s. Multiple RCTs show omega-3 supplementation reduces RA disease activity, decreases NSAID requirements, and lowers morning stiffness. Anti-inflammatory by reducing prostaglandins and leukotrienes.
items.frequency: 2-3 servings per week

items.food: Flaxseeds, Chia seeds, Hemp seeds (ground)
items.benefit: Plant sources of ALA omega-3; converted to EPA/DHA (less efficient); anti-inflammatory; fibre for gut health
items.frequency: Daily — 1-2 tablespoons in smoothies, yogurt, oatmeal

items.food: Walnuts
items.benefit: Highest nut content of ALA omega-3; plus polyphenols (ellagic acid) with anti-inflammatory properties; reduces CRP in RA
items.frequency: Daily — 1 small handful (about 7 walnuts)

items.food: Extra virgin olive oil
items.benefit: Oleocanthal — inhibits COX enzymes (similar mechanism to ibuprofen); oleic acid reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines; monounsaturated fat reduces cardiovascular risk (important in RA and gout)
items.frequency: Daily — use as primary cooking fat and dressing; 2-4 tablespoons/day

items.food: Colourful vegetables: Spinach, Kale, Broccoli, Bell peppers, Tomatoes, Carrots, Sweet potato
items.benefit: Rich in antioxidants (Vitamin C, E, beta-carotene), polyphenols, and Vitamin K; reduce oxidative stress in joints; tomatoes and peppers contain lycopene and vitamin C which support collagen synthesis
items.frequency: 7-9 servings daily; aim for variety of colours

items.food: Berries: Blueberries, Strawberries, Cherries, Blackberries, Raspberries
items.benefit: Tart cherries and cherry juice: strong clinical evidence for reducing gout flares — anthocyanins block uric acid production and reduce inflammation. All berries: anthocyanins and quercetin reduce inflammatory cytokines in RA
items.frequency: Daily — especially tart cherry juice 8 oz/day for gout

items.food: Legumes: Lentils, Chickpeas, Black beans, Kidney beans
items.benefit: Low-fat protein source; high fibre reduces CRP and inflammatory markers; plant-based protein avoids uric acid elevation (unlike animal purines in gout); magnesium and folate
items.frequency: 3-5 times per week

items.food: Whole grains: Oats, Brown rice, Quinoa, Whole wheat, Barley
items.benefit: Fibre reduces inflammatory cytokines and improves gut microbiome health; B vitamins; magnesium; low glycaemic index reduces obesity risk
items.frequency: Daily with each main meal

items.food: Turmeric (curcumin)
items.benefit: Curcumin inhibits NF-κB, COX-2, and TNF-α — key inflammatory pathways in RA and OA. Multiple clinical trials show curcumin supplementation reduces RA disease activity and OA pain. Bioavailability enhanced with black pepper (piperine).
items.frequency: Daily in cooking, warm milk (golden milk), or supplement (500-1000 mg curcumin twice daily with food)

items.food: Ginger
items.benefit: 6-gingerol and 6-shogaol inhibit COX-1, COX-2, and 5-lipoxygenase; reduces joint pain and swelling in OA and RA; anti-nausea (useful for MTX-induced nausea)
items.frequency: Daily in cooking, tea, or supplement (1-2g dried ginger daily)

items.food: Garlic (Allicin)
items.benefit: Anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory; sulfur compounds reduce oxidative stress in joints; inhibits pro-inflammatory cytokine production
items.frequency: Daily — 1-2 cloves in cooking (crush and rest 10 minutes before cooking to activate allicin)

items.food: Cinnamon
items.benefit: Cinnamaldehyde inhibits arachidonic acid release and prostaglandin synthesis; reduces inflammatory biomarkers; improves insulin sensitivity (benefits comorbid diabetes in arthritis)
items.frequency: 1/2-1 tsp daily in oatmeal, warm drinks, smoothies

recommended_foods.category: Vitamin D and Calcium Rich Foods (Bone Protection — essential on steroids)

items.food: Fatty fish, fortified dairy or plant milk, egg yolks, UV-exposed mushrooms
items.benefit: Vitamin D deficiency common in RA and AS; Vit D modulates autoimmune response; essential for calcium absorption; steroid-induced osteoporosis prevention
items.frequency: Daily; supplement 1000-2000 IU Vitamin D3 if levels below 30 ng/mL

items.food: Calcium: dairy products, fortified plant milk, green leafy vegetables, almonds, sesame seeds (tahini)
items.benefit: Bone density maintenance — critically important in patients on long-term corticosteroids and in postmenopausal women with RA or AS
items.frequency: Target 1000-1200 mg calcium daily from diet and supplements combined

items.food: Eggs (whole), Low-fat dairy: yogurt, skimmed milk, cottage cheese
items.benefit: Low-purine high-quality protein sources. Dairy consumption is associated with LOWER gout risk — dairy proteins promote renal uric acid excretion. Yogurt probiotics reduce systemic inflammation.
items.frequency: Daily — especially low-fat dairy as primary protein source in gout

items.food: Chicken and turkey (moderate portions), tofu
items.benefit: Lower purine content than red meat and organ meats; tofu and plant proteins do not raise uric acid despite moderate purine content
items.frequency: Moderate — 1-2 servings daily; keep portions controlled (100-150g)

items.food: Tart cherry juice or fresh tart cherries
items.benefit: Strongest dietary evidence for gout: reduces serum uric acid, reduces gout flare frequency by 35% in RCTs; anthocyanins inhibit xanthine oxidase and reduce inflammation
items.frequency: 240 mL (8 oz) tart cherry juice daily; or 10-12 tart cherries daily during active gout

items.food: Vitamin C-rich foods: Citrus fruits, bell peppers, kiwi, guava, strawberries, broccoli
items.benefit: Vitamin C is essential for collagen synthesis (hydroxylation of proline and lysine); reduces oxidative stress in joint cartilage; associated with slower OA progression
items.frequency: Daily — 2-3 servings; target 75-90 mg Vitamin C/day minimum

items.food: Bone broth (collagen-rich)
items.benefit: Contains type II collagen, glycine, proline, hydroxyproline; may support cartilage health in OA; emerging evidence for joint pain reduction
items.frequency: 1-2 cups daily as dietary supplement; especially for OA

items.food: Pomegranate juice
items.benefit: Ellagic acid blocks enzymes that cause cartilage degradation in OA; reduces IL-1β and TNF-α production; high antioxidant content
items.frequency: Small glass (100-150 mL) daily or alternate days

foods_to_avoid.reason: Purines are metabolized to uric acid. High purine intake raises serum uric acid levels, directly triggering gout attacks and worsening hyperuricemia.
examples: Organ meats (liver, kidney, sweetbreads, brain) — highest purine content
Red meat in large quantities (beef, lamb, pork)
Anchovies, herring, mackerel, sardines, sprats (purine-rich oily fish)
Beer and ale (yeast and alcohol combined — most potent gout trigger)

foods_to_avoid.reason: Alcohol raises uric acid by increasing purine breakdown and reducing renal uric acid excretion. Beer contains guanosine (purine) as well as alcohol. Spirits raise uric acid more than wine. All alcohol worsens gout and increases inflammation in RA and OA.
examples: Excessive wine (moderate wine consumption less harmful for gout)
All types of alcohol worsen inflammatory arthritis

foods_to_avoid.reason: Fructose metabolism generates purines (AMP) and elevates uric acid. High fructose intake is strongly associated with hyperuricemia and gout — independent of overall calorie intake. Major hidden gout trigger.
examples: Sugary beverages (sodas, fizzy drinks — largest source of HFCS)
Packaged sweets, candy, high-fructose corn syrup in processed foods

foods_to_avoid.reason: High in trans fats, omega-6 fatty acids, refined carbohydrates, and additives that promote systemic inflammation. Directly worsen inflammatory arthritis (RA, PsA, AS) and contribute to obesity (worsens OA).
High in saturated fats (pro-inflammatory; elevate IL-6, TNF-α); high purine content worsens gout; processed meats (nitrates, nitrites, sodium) increase systemic inflammation and cardiovascular risk.
examples: Processed meats: sausages, bacon, salami, hot dogs, deli meats
Red meat in large portions: beef, lamb, pork

foods_to_avoid.reason: Spike blood glucose and insulin; promote AGE (advanced glycation end-product) formation damaging cartilage; increase NF-κB inflammatory pathway; contribute to obesity — major arthritis risk factor.

The Western diet has an imbalanced omega-6 to omega-3 ratio (~15:1; ideal <4:1). Excess omega-6 (arachidonic acid pathway) promotes prostaglandin and leukotriene production, driving joint inflammation in RA and OA.

High sodium promotes hypertension and cardiovascular risk (already elevated in RA); may enhance inflammatory response; worsens fluid retention and edema around inflamed joints; high sodium intake linked to autoimmune activation.
examples: Soy sauce and other salty condiments

foods_to_avoid.food: Dairy — only in those with sensitivity (not universal avoidance)
foods_to_avoid.reason: Some people with inflammatory arthritis report symptom worsening with full-fat dairy. However, low-fat dairy is beneficial in gout. The concern is more about full-fat, high-saturated-fat dairy products.
examples: Full-fat milk and cream (in large quantities)
Note: low-fat dairy (yogurt, skimmed milk) is actually beneficial for gout — do not restrict
foods_to_avoid.nuance: Low-fat dairy reduces uric acid and gout risk; do not universally avoid dairy; consider full-fat dairy restriction only if personally symptomatic

foods_to_avoid.food: Nightshade vegetables (controversial — only for some patients)
foods_to_avoid.reason: Some arthritis patients (OA, RA) anecdotally report worsening with nightshade vegetables. Scientific evidence is limited and inconclusive. Not universally recommended for avoidance.
foods_to_avoid.nuance: These vegetables have strong anti-inflammatory properties for most people. Only avoid if personally identified as a trigger through food diary. Bell peppers and tomatoes have high Vitamin C (beneficial for arthritis generally).

sample_meal_plan.note: This general anti-inflammatory, joint-supportive meal plan is based on Mediterranean dietary principles. Gout patients must follow additional low-purine modifications. Individual needs vary — consult a registered dietitian and rheumatologist.
sample_meal_plan.early_morning: Warm water with lemon (Vitamin C, alkalizing) + 2-3 soaked walnuts + 1 Brazil nut (selenium) + 1 tsp ground turmeric with black pepper in warm water
sample_meal_plan.breakfast: Oatmeal with blueberries, ground flaxseed, and cinnamon OR whole grain toast with avocado and 2 boiled eggs + 1 cup green tea (light brew)
sample_meal_plan.mid_morning: 1 orange or kiwi + small handful mixed nuts (walnuts, almonds) OR 120 mL tart cherry juice (for gout patients)
sample_meal_plan.lunch: Grilled salmon (or tuna) with quinoa and steamed broccoli with olive oil and garlic + large colourful salad (spinach, bell pepper, tomatoes, cucumber) with extra virgin olive oil and lemon dressing + 1 cup low-fat yogurt
sample_meal_plan.evening_snack: Apple with 1 tbsp almond butter OR vegetable sticks (carrot, celery, cucumber) with hummus + 1 cup ginger tea with honey
sample_meal_plan.dinner: Grilled chicken or paneer (or lentil curry for plant-based) + brown rice or whole wheat chapati + stir-fried kale/spinach with garlic and olive oil + turmeric golden milk before bed
sample_meal_plan.before_bed: Golden milk (warm milk / plant milk + 1/2 tsp turmeric + pinch black pepper + honey)

special_dietary_notes: Weight management is critical — every kg lost reduces knee joint load by 4 kg. Even 5-10% body weight reduction significantly reduces OA pain and NSAIDs requirement.

Mediterranean diet is the most evidence-based pattern for arthritis: abundant vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, olive oil, fish; moderate poultry and dairy; limited red meat and processed foods.
Gout patients: maintain uric acid target <6 mg/dL through diet + urate-lowering medication. Diet alone reduces uric acid by 1-2 mg/dL — medication usually required for sustained control.
Maintain adequate hydration (8-10 glasses water daily) — dehydration triggers gout attacks by concentrating uric acid; promotes joint lubrication; dilutes inflammatory mediators.

Omega-3 supplementation (fish oil): 2-4g EPA+DHA daily — meta-analyses support reduction in RA disease activity scores and NSAID requirements. Use enteric-coated fish oil capsules to reduce GI side effects.

Patients on methotrexate: ensure adequate folate intake (folate-rich foods: leafy greens, legumes, fortified cereals) and folic acid supplement as prescribed; limit alcohol completely (increases hepatotoxicity).

Patients on corticosteroids: increase calcium and Vitamin D intake; restrict sodium and refined sugars (reduce steroid-related weight gain and edema); increase potassium-rich foods (bananas, sweet potato, leafy greens).
Vitamin D supplementation: ensure serum 25(OH)D >30 ng/mL; supplement 1000-2000 IU Vitamin D3 daily if deficient; Vitamin D deficiency worsens autoimmune arthritis and increases fracture risk.

exercise_and_physical_therapy.overview: Exercise is the single most evidence-based non-pharmacological treatment for all forms of arthritis. Regular appropriate exercise reduces pain, improves joint function, strengthens muscles that protect joints, reduces fatigue, and improves mental health. 'Motion is lotion for joints.'

examples: Swimming and aquatic exercise (best for OA — water buoyancy offloads joints; warm water reduces stiffness)
Cycling (stationary or outdoor — low impact; excellent for knee OA)
recommended_exercises.frequency: 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise per week (30 minutes x 5 days)
recommended_exercises.benefit: Reduces joint pain and stiffness; improves cardiovascular health (critical in RA with higher CV risk); promotes weight management; releases endorphins

recommended_exercises.frequency: 2-3 times per week; rest days between sessions
recommended_exercises.benefit: Strengthens muscles around joints reducing load on articular cartilage; improves joint stability; prevents falls and fractures; reduces disability in RA and OA

examples: Gentle joint range of motion exercises (daily — especially hands, wrists, knees)
Yoga — modified for arthritis; evidence for pain reduction in OA and RA
recommended_exercises.frequency: Daily — 5-10 minutes morning (especially important to reduce morning stiffness in RA)
recommended_exercises.benefit: Maintains and improves joint mobility; reduces morning stiffness duration; prevents contractures

examples: Tai Chi — very strong evidence for OA, RA, and AS; reduces pain, fall risk, and improves balance
recommended_exercises.benefit: Reduces fall risk (critical in elderly with arthritis on multiple medications); improves proprioception; reduces fear of movement

precautions: Exercise through MILD discomfort (2/10 pain) is acceptable — stop if pain is severe (>5/10) or worsening after 24 hours
Exercise in warm water or heated pools during flares — reduces pain while maintaining movement
During acute inflammatory flares (RA, gout): rest acutely inflamed joints; range-of-motion exercises for other joints only
Apply heat to joints before exercise to reduce stiffness; apply ice after exercise to reduce inflammation
Always warm up 5-10 minutes before exercise; cool down gradually
Work with physiotherapist for individualized exercise prescription
Monitor for worsening fatigue in RA — pacing strategies essential

joint_protection_strategies: Use ergonomic assistive devices — jar openers, key turners, long-handled reachers, electric can openers (reduce hand joint strain in RA/OA hand)
Wear prescribed orthotic insoles in shoes — redistributes weight bearing on knee joints; reduces OA knee pain by 25-50%
Use knee bracing or knee sleeve — provides warmth, stability, and proprioceptive feedback in knee OA
Thumb splints for first CMC joint OA — reduces base of thumb pain during pinch activities
Wrist splints (especially night-use) for wrist RA — reduce pain and maintain functional wrist position
Walking aids (cane in contralateral hand, walking frame) — significantly reduces knee and hip joint load
Use larger, stronger joints for heavier tasks — carry bags on forearm not fingers; push doors with shoulder not fingers
Avoid staying in same position for prolonged periods — micro-breaks every 30-45 minutes; change positions
Ergonomic workplace assessment — raised chair, keyboard positioning, anti-fatigue matting
Adequate footwear — cushioned, wide-fitting shoes with good arch support; avoid high heels (increases knee load by 23%)

heat_therapy.benefits: Reduces morning stiffness and chronic pain; relaxes muscles; improves flexibility; increases local circulation
methods: Warm shower or bath — especially effective for morning stiffness; 15-20 minutes
Electric heating pad or heat wrap
Warm wax bath (paraffin bath) for hand OA — deeply penetrating warmth for small joints
Warm compress or hot water bottle
heat_therapy.when_to_use: Chronic stiffness, before exercise, muscle spasm, OA pain — NOT during active hot inflammatory flare

cold_therapy.benefits: Reduces acute inflammation, swelling, and pain; numbs acute pain; reduces post-exercise soreness
methods: Ice pack wrapped in cloth (never apply ice directly to skin)
Frozen peas or corn bag — conforms to joint
cold_therapy.when_to_use: During acute inflammatory flares (gout, RA flare); immediately after injury; post-exercise swelling
cold_therapy.duration: 15-20 minutes; at least 45 minutes between applications; protect skin from frostbite

trigger_avoidance: For gout: avoid beer, spirits, organ meats, shellfish, high-fructose beverages; maintain hydration (3L fluid daily); avoid fasting or crash dieting (raises uric acid); monitor and manage medications that raise uric acid (thiazide diuretics, low-dose aspirin)

For RA and autoimmune arthritis: avoid smoking (strongest environmental risk factor for RA onset and severity; reduces drug efficacy); manage psychological stress; avoid infections by vaccination and good hygiene
For OA: avoid high-impact activities (jumping, running on hard surfaces) in advanced joint disease; manage body weight
For AS: avoid prolonged immobility and bed rest (paradoxically worsens AS); sleep on firm mattress without pillow under knees
General: protect joints from repeated trauma and overuse; proper technique for lifting and physical tasks
mental_health_and_wellbeing: Chronic pain counselling or CBT (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy) — most effective psychological intervention for chronic arthritis pain management; addresses pain catastrophizing and fear-avoidance behavior
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) — evidence-based for chronic pain; improves function and quality of life
Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) — reduces pain, improves sleep, reduces anxiety and depression in arthritis
Join arthritis patient support groups (Arthritis Foundation, Versus Arthritis UK, NRAS — National Rheumatoid Arthritis Society) for peer support, education, and wellbeing programs
Pain management programs — multidisciplinary inpatient or outpatient programs combining physiotherapy, occupational therapy, psychology, and pain medicine

Adequate sleep — chronic pain severely disrupts sleep; sleep disorders worsen pain perception; address sleep hygiene, consider sleep study if sleep apnoea suspected (OA patients with obesity at high risk)
Maintain social connections and employment where possible — social isolation and unemployment worsen chronic pain and depression
Set realistic functional goals with healthcare team — 'treat-to-target' approach in RA; functional independence goals in OA

arthritis_monitoring_plan.note: Arthritis monitoring is based on disease activity scores, symptom assessment, functional status, and laboratory markers. Below is a practical guide to when action is needed.

green_zone.oa_criteria: Pain ≤2/10; performing most activities; NSAIDs or paracetamol needed occasionally or not at all
green_zone.ra_criteria: DAS28 <2.6 (remission) or <3.2 (low disease activity); no swollen joints; CRP and ESR normal or near normal; HAQ improving; no active synovitis on ultrasound
green_zone.gout_criteria: No flares in past 6-12 months; serum uric acid <6 mg/dL; no growing tophi
green_zone.action: Continue current treatment regimen. Regular follow-up every 3-6 months. Maintain healthy lifestyle, exercise program, and dietary recommendations.

yellow_zone.oa_criteria: Pain 3-6/10; daily NSAIDs required; difficulty with stairs, walking, or ADLs; considering joint injection
yellow_zone.ra_criteria: DAS28 3.2-5.1 (moderate disease activity); new or increasing joint swelling; rising CRP/ESR; morning stiffness >30-60 minutes
yellow_zone.gout_criteria: 1-2 flares in past 6 months; serum uric acid 6-8 mg/dL; stable tophi
yellow_zone.action: Contact rheumatologist or physician within 2-4 weeks. Medication adjustment likely needed — increase DMARD dose, add combination therapy, or consider biologic. Review lifestyle factors, diet, and adherence. X-ray or ultrasound may be required.

red_zone.status: Severe Flare / Medical Emergency / Rapid Deterioration
red_zone.oa_criteria: Pain 7-10/10; unable to walk or perform self-care; suspect mechanical joint failure or fracture
red_zone.ra_criteria: DAS28 >5.1 (high disease activity); multiple swollen/tender joints; elevated CRP >50 mg/L; new rheumatoid nodules; new systemic features (fever, pleurisy, vasculitis); suspected DMARD side effect (agranulocytosis, hepatitis)
red_zone.gout_criteria: Severe acute gout attack with fever; multiple joint involvement; suspected joint infection (septic arthritis) — EMERGENCY
red_zone.septic_arthritis_emergency: Single hot, red, swollen joint with fever — IMMEDIATE hospital assessment. Joint aspiration and IV antibiotics must not be delayed — joint destruction within 24-48 hours.
red_zone.action: URGENT medical attention required. Contact rheumatologist immediately for RA flares. For single hot joint with fever — go to emergency department immediately (possible septic arthritis — medical emergency). For AS with neurological symptoms — emergency spinal imaging required.

complications.description: Progressive cartilage loss (OA) or immune-mediated joint erosion (RA, PsA) leads to irreversible structural damage, malalignment, and deformity. In RA: ulnar deviation, swan neck, boutonniere, Z-thumb, hammer toe deformities. In OA: valgus/varus knee deformity, osteophytes.
complications.severity: Moderate to Severe — permanent without surgical correction
complications.prevention: Early treatment in inflammatory arthritis; treat-to-target strategy; weight management in OA

complications.description: Life-threatening emergency. Bacterial infection of a joint — most commonly Staphylococcus aureus. Destroys articular cartilage within 24-72 hours if untreated. Presents as single very hot, swollen, painful joint with fever. Requires emergency joint aspiration, culture, and IV antibiotics.
complications.risk_factors: RA patients, prosthetic joints, immunosuppressed (on biologics/DMARDs), IV drug users, elderly, diabetics

complications.description: RA is an independent cardiovascular risk factor — equivalent to Type 2 diabetes. Systemic inflammation accelerates atherosclerosis; incidence of MI and stroke 1.5-2x higher in RA vs general population. Gout is associated with hypertension, metabolic syndrome, and cardiovascular events.
complications.severity: Severe — major cause of mortality in RA
complications.management: Aggressive CV risk factor modification; statins; blood pressure management; smoking cessation; aspirin where appropriate; effective RA treatment reduces CV risk

complications.description: Systemic inflammation, immobility, and long-term corticosteroid use cause severe bone density loss. RA patients have 2x higher hip fracture risk. AS causes vertebral fractures. Gout patients have higher osteoporosis prevalence.
complications.management: Calcium 1000-1200 mg/day + Vitamin D 800-2000 IU/day; weight-bearing exercise; bisphosphonates if T-score <-2.5 or on long-term steroids; DEXA monitoring

complications.description: Occurs in 10-40% of RA patients; can precede joint disease. Immune-mediated inflammation in lung interstitium causes progressive fibrosis, cough, and breathlessness. Also associated with some DMARDs (methotrexate pneumonitis — rare).
complications.management: Pulmonary function tests and HRCT at diagnosis; pulmonology referral; mycophenolate or azathioprine for RA-ILD; stop causative DMARD if suspected drug-induced

complications.description: Anterior uveitis (iritis) is a common extra-articular feature of AS (25-40%), JIA (30%), and reactive arthritis. Presents as sudden painful red eye with photophobia and blurred vision. Can cause glaucoma, cataracts, and vision loss if untreated.
complications.management: Urgent ophthalmology assessment; topical steroid eye drops; mydriatic drops; systemic TNF inhibitors dramatically reduce uveitis frequency in AS

complications.description: Carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve compression from wrist synovitis in RA); cervical myelopathy from atlanto-axial subluxation in severe RA; peripheral vasculitis-related neuropathy in severe RA.
complications.management: Wrist splints for CTS; nerve conduction studies; surgical decompression if severe; cervical spine MRI and stabilization surgery for atlanto-axial subluxation

complications.description: Gout causes uric acid kidney stones and gouty nephropathy (urate deposits in renal parenchyma) with chronic kidney disease. NSAIDs and cyclosporine (used in PsA) are nephrotoxic. Some biologics require dose adjustment in renal impairment.
complications.management: Monitor renal function regularly; adequate hydration for gout; avoid prolonged NSAIDs; allopurinol dose adjustment by eGFR

complications.complication: Chronic Pain Syndrome and Central Sensitization
complications.description: Chronic joint pain leads to central sensitization — amplified pain perception from neuroplastic changes in pain-processing pathways. Results in widespread pain beyond joint involvement, allodynia, and hyperalgesia. Often mistaken for inadequate disease control in RA.
complications.severity: Moderate — significantly impacts quality of life
complications.management: Pain psychology (CBT, ACT); duloxetine or low-dose amitriptyline for central sensitization; pain management programs; mindfulness

complications.description: Affects 30-40% of people with chronic arthritis. Bidirectional relationship — pain and disability cause depression; depression amplifies pain perception and reduces treatment adherence. Associated with worse arthritis outcomes.
