complications.management: Screen with PHQ-9 and GAD-7; CBT most effective treatment; antidepressants (SNRIs have dual benefit for pain); treat underlying arthritis effectively; social support; exercise

key_points: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) is the most common chronic arthritis in children — affects 1 in 1000 children under 16
Early diagnosis and treatment critical — prevents joint destruction, maintains normal growth and development, prevents visual loss from silent uveitis
Biannual slit-lamp eye examination essential in oligoarticular JIA (uveitis is often asymptomatic but vision-threatening)
NSAIDs (naproxen or ibuprofen) are first-line for symptom control; methotrexate SC for polyarticular disease
Biologic therapy (etanercept, adalimumab, tocilizumab, abatacept) available for refractory JIA — significantly improved long-term outcomes
School accommodation letter essential — explain stiffness, fatigue, inability to write long periods, need for mobility breaks
Physical therapy, occupational therapy, and psychology support integral to JIA management
Systemic JIA (Still's disease) with rash, high spiking fever, lymphadenopathy — anakinra or canakinumab (IL-1 inhibitors) first-line
Splints and orthoses to maintain joint alignment and prevent contractures
Transitional care planning essential at age 16-18 — transition to adult rheumatology services should be carefully managed
RA commonly improves during pregnancy (70% — immune tolerance of pregnancy) but frequently flares severely 3-6 months postpartum
PsA behavior in pregnancy is variable; AS may improve or worsen
NSAIDs: use lowest effective dose; avoid in third trimester (premature ductus arteriosus closure, delayed labour); single doses acceptable second trimester
Hydroxychloroquine: safe in pregnancy — continue (prevents postpartum flares); also reduces risk of neonatal lupus
Methotrexate: ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED — stop 3-6 months before conception; men should also stop 3 months before fathering children
Leflunomide: CONTRAINDICATED — very long half-life; cholestyramine washout procedure required
Sulfasalazine: generally safe in pregnancy; ensure folic acid 5mg daily; men — may cause reversible oligospermia
Prednisolone (low dose): relatively safe; use lowest effective dose; slight risk of cleft palate in 1st trimester with high doses

TNF inhibitors: generally compatible with first and second trimesters; stop adalimumab/infliximab/etanercept at 28-32 weeks to reduce fetal drug exposure and vaccine timing issues for infant (live vaccines delayed)
Certolizumab pegol: unique biologic with minimal placental transfer — considered throughout pregnancy if needed
Collaborate with obstetrics, rheumatology, and pharmacy for individualized medication management throughout pregnancy
OA is the dominant arthritis type in elderly — affects 80% of adults over 75 on X-ray
Polypharmacy risk — NSAIDs particularly dangerous in elderly (GI bleeding, renal impairment, hypertension, heart failure)
Prefer topical NSAIDs, paracetamol, intra-articular corticosteroid injections, or hyaluronic acid over oral NSAIDs in elderly
Increased infection risk on DMARDs and biologics — pneumococcal and influenza vaccination essential
RA in elderly may present as 'elderly-onset RA' (EORA) — often RF-negative, involves large joints, marked constitutional symptoms
PMR (Polymyalgia Rheumatica) frequently presents as RA mimic in elderly — bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain with high ESR; responds dramatically to prednisolone 15-20 mg
Fall risk assessment essential — joint pain, muscle weakness, and medications (opioids, sedatives) increase fall and fracture risk
Renal dose adjustment required for many medications (NSAIDs, colchicine, allopurinol, methotrexate, biologics)
Geriatric assessment for frailty, cognitive function, and social support — impacts treatment decisions and adherence
Physiotherapy crucial for muscle strengthening and fall prevention
Patients on biologic DMARDs (TNF inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, rituximab) are significantly immunocompromised — high infection risk
Mandatory pre-biologic screening: TB (Mantoux or IGRA), hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, VZV immunity
Annual flu vaccination and pneumococcal vaccination required — use inactivated vaccines only
No live vaccines while on immunosuppressive therapy (LAIV flu spray, yellow fever, MMR, varicella, shingles — AVOID)
Shingles vaccine (Shingrix — inactivated, 2 doses): recommended BEFORE starting JAK inhibitors; high herpes zoster risk on tofacitinib and upadacitinib
Suspend biologic/DMARD therapy for significant infections and surgery
Latent TB: full course of isoniazid or rifampicin prophylaxis before starting biologic therapy
Septic arthritis risk higher — any hot, swollen single joint must be aspirated urgently regardless of DMARD history

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Annually before flu season (October/November in northern hemisphere)
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Influenza infections can trigger RA and PsA flares; patients on DMARDs/biologics have impaired immunity; flu worsens reactive arthritis; annual vaccination strongly recommended for all arthritis patients on immunosuppressive therapy
vaccinations_recommended.note: Use inactivated vaccine only — LAIV (live attenuated nasal spray) contraindicated in immunosuppressed patients

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: PCV20 or PCV15 single dose; followed by PPSV23 at least 1 year later; booster at 65 if given before 65
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Patients on immunosuppressive therapy have increased risk of invasive pneumococcal disease (pneumonia, meningitis, septicaemia); DMARDs and biologics impair B-cell response to pneumococcal antigens

vaccinations_recommended.vaccine: Herpes Zoster Vaccine (Shingrix — Recombinant Zoster Vaccine, RZV)
vaccinations_recommended.reason: JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib) and some biologics significantly increase herpes zoster (shingles) risk. Shingrix is a recombinant (non-live) vaccine safe for immunosuppressed patients. Administer BEFORE starting JAK inhibitors if possible.
vaccinations_recommended.note: Old live Zostavax vaccine is contraindicated in immunosuppressed patients — use Shingrix only

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: As per current national guidelines — annual booster for immunosuppressed
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Arthritis patients on biologics and DMARDs at higher risk of severe COVID-19; COVID-19 infection can trigger arthritis flares; vaccine-induced immunity may be suboptimal in heavily immunosuppressed patients (additional doses may be recommended)

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 3-dose series (0, 1, 6 months) for non-immune patients; check serology post-vaccination
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Rituximab and some other biologics can reactivate hepatitis B causing fulminant hepatitis; hepatitis B vaccination before starting biologic therapy is essential if seronegative

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Per national schedule (ideally before 26 years; consider up to 45 years in immunosuppressed)
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Patients on immunosuppressive therapy have impaired immune control of HPV, increasing cervical cancer risk (in women) and other HPV-related cancers; regular cervical cancer screening (Pap smear/HPV test) is essential in RA women
Routine adult immunisation; pertussis (whooping cough) can complicate respiratory function; surgical procedures common in arthritis management — ensure tetanus protection

vaccinations_recommended.vaccine: Varicella (Chickenpox) Vaccine — only if non-immune and NOT yet on immunosuppression
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Non-immune arthritis patients should receive varicella vaccine BEFORE starting biologics or DMARDs. Live vaccine — CONTRAINDICATED once on immunosuppressive therapy.
vaccinations_recommended.note: Check VZV IgG serology; vaccinate seronegative patients before starting immunosuppressive therapy

when_to_see_doctor: Joint pain lasting more than 6 weeks without clear injury cause — persistent arthralgia warrants rheumatological assessment
Morning stiffness lasting more than 30-60 minutes — hallmark of inflammatory arthritis requiring urgent rheumatology referral
Symmetrical joint swelling — especially small joints of hands (MCP, PIP joints) and wrists — possible early RA
Single hot, red, swollen joint with fever — URGENT: same-day assessment to exclude septic arthritis (joint destruction within 24-48h)
Sudden severe big toe or ankle pain at night in men with or without prior gout diagnosis — possible gout attack
New back pain in young adult (under 40) that improves with exercise but worsens with rest — possible ankylosing spondylitis
Joint symptoms with skin rash — butterfly rash (lupus), psoriatic plaques (PsA), or salmon-colored rash with fever in a child (systemic JIA)
Eye redness, pain, or blurred vision in a patient with arthritis — uveitis or episcleritis (same-day ophthalmology referral)
New or worsening breathlessness or cough in RA patient — possible interstitial lung disease or pleural effusion
Worsening disease activity despite current medications — DMARD dose adjustment or add-on therapy needed

Side effects from arthritis medications — skin rash or sore throat on antithyroid drugs (agranulocytosis); jaundice on MTX or leflunomide; chest pain on NSAIDs; signs of serious infection on biologics
Planning pregnancy while on DMARDs — medication review ESSENTIAL before conception (MTX, leflunomide are teratogenic)
Significant functional decline — difficulty with self-care, work, or daily activities despite treatment
Annual review even if well-controlled: monitor for disease progression, medication side effects, cardiovascular risk, bone density, and vaccination status
emergency_signs: Single hot, red, extremely swollen, painful joint with fever — septic arthritis until proven otherwise — EMERGENCY (go to ER immediately; hours matter for joint survival)
Sudden severe unilateral hip or groin pain with inability to weight bear — avascular necrosis, hip fracture, or septic hip joint — EMERGENCY
New onset neurological symptoms in RA patient — neck pain with hand/arm tingling, weakness, or difficulty walking — atlanto-axial subluxation (C1-C2 cord compression) — EMERGENCY spinal imaging
New onset severe back pain with leg weakness, numbness, or bladder/bowel dysfunction in AS patient — cord compression — EMERGENCY
Fever and severe illness while on biologic therapy (TNF inhibitor, JAK inhibitor, rituximab) — serious opportunistic infection (TB, fungal, bacterial sepsis) — EMERGENCY
Sudden severe eye pain, photophobia, and vision change in AS or JIA patient — acute uveitis — same-day ophthalmology EMERGENCY
Rapidly spreading skin rash with fever on allopurinol — possible severe cutaneous reaction (Stevens-Johnson Syndrome/DRESS) — STOP drug immediately, go to ER
Chest pain, breathlessness, leg swelling, and calf pain while on JAK inhibitor — possible pulmonary embolism or DVT (thromboembolism) — EMERGENCY
Severe acute abdominal pain while on NSAIDs — possible GI perforation or major upper GI bleed — EMERGENCY
Severe weakness, jaundice, or confusion in patient on methotrexate — possible hepatotoxicity or bone marrow suppression — EMERGENCY blood tests and stop medication

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is arthritis curable?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Most forms of arthritis cannot be cured but can be very effectively managed. Osteoarthritis (OA) — the wear-and-tear type — cannot be reversed, but symptoms can be greatly reduced and progression slowed. Inflammatory arthritis (RA, PsA, AS) can achieve clinical remission with modern treatment — meaning no active inflammation, though the autoimmune tendency remains. Septic arthritis can be cured with appropriate antibiotics. Gout can be effectively prevented with urate-lowering therapy.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a degenerative 'wear and tear' disease of cartilage — not primarily autoimmune. Pain worsens with activity and is usually asymmetric. It affects older adults. Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks the joint lining — causing symmetrical small joint involvement, morning stiffness >1 hour, and elevated inflammation markers. RA can affect any age and involves systemic complications. RA requires disease-modifying treatment (DMARDs/biologics) while OA is managed with symptom relief, exercise, and joint replacement.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Does diet affect arthritis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes, significantly. A Mediterranean-style diet rich in omega-3 fatty acids (fish, walnuts, flaxseed), anti-inflammatory spices (turmeric, ginger), colourful vegetables, and olive oil reduces inflammation in RA and OA. For gout, reducing purine-rich foods (organ meats, shellfish, beer) and fructose is essential for controlling uric acid. Weight loss through diet reduces knee OA pain by significantly reducing joint load. Fish oil supplements (2-4g EPA+DHA daily) have demonstrated clinical benefit in RA.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is exercise safe for arthritis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Exercise is not only safe — it is one of the most effective treatments for arthritis. Regular physical activity reduces joint pain, improves function, strengthens protective muscles, reduces fatigue, and benefits mental health. Swimming, cycling, walking, yoga, and Tai Chi are particularly beneficial. The key is choosing appropriate exercise (low-impact aerobic for OA; range of motion + strengthening for RA) and working with a physiotherapist for personalized guidance. Rest during acute flares, but keep moving otherwise — 'motion is lotion for joints.'

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is gout and how is it different from other arthritis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Gout is a crystal-induced arthritis caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints from high uric acid levels (hyperuricemia). It presents as sudden, exquisitely painful flares — typically in the big toe — with redness, swelling, and heat. Between flares, patients are completely symptom-free (unlike OA/RA). Diagnosis is confirmed by needle-shaped crystals in joint fluid. Gout is managed with NSAIDs or colchicine for attacks, and allopurinol long-term to reduce uric acid. Diet (avoiding purines and alcohol) is a critical management component.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is methotrexate and why is it used for arthritis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Methotrexate (MTX) is the cornerstone 'anchor' treatment for rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis. It is a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) that reduces joint inflammation, prevents cartilage and bone erosion, and slows disease progression. Taken once weekly (with folic acid to reduce side effects), it typically takes 6-12 weeks to show benefit. It requires regular blood test monitoring. It is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What are biologic drugs for arthritis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Biologics are advanced targeted medicines (monoclonal antibodies or fusion proteins) that block specific inflammatory molecules driving joint destruction. The most commonly used class is anti-TNF agents (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab) which block tumor necrosis factor-alpha. Other targets include IL-6 (tocilizumab), IL-17 (secukinumab), IL-23 (guselkumab), T-cells (abatacept), and B-cells (rituximab). Biologics are used for moderate-severe RA, PsA, and AS not responding to conventional DMARDs. They require infection screening (TB, hepatitis B) before starting and increase infection risk.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How is gout treated during an acute attack?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: During an acute gout attack: (1) Rest the affected joint; apply ice; elevate the limb. (2) Take colchicine 1mg then 0.5mg 1 hour later (low-dose regimen) as early as possible — most effective when started within 12-24 hours. Or take an NSAID (indomethacin 50mg three times daily, naproxen 500mg twice daily) — equally effective. Or oral prednisolone 30-40mg/day for 5 days if NSAIDs and colchicine are contraindicated. Do NOT start allopurinol during an attack — it can prolong the flare. Start allopurinol 2-4 weeks after the attack has resolved.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can arthritis affect organs other than joints?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — especially inflammatory arthritis. RA can cause interstitial lung disease, pleuritis and pericarditis, eye inflammation (episcleritis, keratokeratitis sicca from Sjögren's overlap), anaemia, vasculitis, and cervical spine instability. Ankylosing Spondylitis causes uveitis (25-40%), aortitis, and restrictive lung disease. Psoriatic arthritis is associated with cardiovascular disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and metabolic syndrome. Gout damages kidneys (uric acid nephropathy, kidney stones). This is why inflammatory arthritis requires specialist care beyond just the joints.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the 'treat-to-target' strategy in rheumatoid arthritis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Treat-to-target (T2T) is a strategy where treatment is adjusted every 1-3 months until a pre-defined target is achieved — usually DAS28 remission (<2.6) or at minimum low disease activity (<3.2). Regular disease activity measurement (DAS28, CDAI, SDAI) guides step-up of treatment when target is not met. This proactive approach dramatically reduces joint erosions, disability, and improves long-term outcomes. Early, intensive treatment in the 'window of opportunity' (first 3-6 months) has the greatest impact on preventing permanent joint damage.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is ankylosing spondylitis and why does the back pain improve with exercise?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory arthritis of the spine and sacroiliac joints. The key distinguishing feature is that unlike mechanical back pain (which worsens with activity), AS back pain IMPROVES with movement and WORSENS with rest and prolonged immobility. This is because movement disperses inflammatory fluid and maintains spinal flexibility. Prolonged bed rest is harmful in AS and accelerates spinal fusion. Daily exercise (swimming, hydrotherapy, specific AS physio exercises) is as important as medication and is essential to maintain spinal posture and mobility.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is it safe to have surgery while on arthritis medications?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Surgery planning in arthritis patients requires careful medication management. Biologic drugs (anti-TNF, tocilizumab, etc.) should be withheld for 1-4 weeks before elective surgery (depending on the specific drug half-life) due to increased infection and wound healing risk. Methotrexate can usually be continued through minor surgery but should be discussed with the surgeon. Low-dose prednisolone should be continued and stress-dose steroids given if on long-term steroids. NSAIDs should be stopped 5-7 days pre-operatively (bleeding and cardiovascular risk). Always inform all surgeons and anaesthetists about all arthritis medications.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Why do some arthritis medications require regular blood tests?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Several arthritis medications carry risks of serious organ toxicity that must be monitored: Methotrexate can cause liver fibrosis and bone marrow suppression — requiring LFTs and CBC every 4-8 weeks initially. Leflunomide is hepatotoxic — requires LFTs. Sulfasalazine can cause bone marrow suppression — requires CBC. NSAIDs reduce kidney blood flow — requires renal function tests. Biologics and JAK inhibitors increase infection risk — require CBC and inflammatory markers. Allopurinol requires renal function tests for dosing. These blood tests allow early detection of side effects before they become serious, ensuring safe treatment.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can I become pregnant while on arthritis medications?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Pregnancy planning in arthritis requires specialist review months in advance. Methotrexate and leflunomide are absolutely contraindicated — stop methotrexate 3-6 months and leflunomide (with washout) months before trying to conceive. Safe medications in pregnancy include hydroxychloroquine (continue — protective), sulfasalazine (with folic acid), low-dose prednisolone, certolizumab pegol (minimal placental transfer), and remdesivir. Most TNF inhibitors should be stopped at 28-32 weeks. NSAIDs should be avoided in the third trimester. Male patients on MTX should also stop 3 months before fathering children.
